facts.fact: Nasion is the junction of the frontal and nasal bones in the midsagittal plane (intersection of internasal and frontonasal sutures per one source).
Glabella is the most prominent/forward midline point of the forehead above the nasal root, at about the level of the supra-orbital ridges.
Orbitale is the lowest point of the orbital margin/inferior orbital rim; with porion it defines the Frankfort horizontal plane (FH = porion-orbitale).
One source defines orbitale differently: as a point midway between the lowest points of the inferior margins of the two orbits, which the source notes affects reproducibility.
Porion is the uppermost point of the external auditory meatus (superior point of the external acoustic opening margin).
Porion and orbitale are described as hard to locate because they sit in a vague region containing soft tissue, nerves and vessels.
Zygion is the most lateral point of the zygomatic arch.
Gonion is the most outward inferior point of the mandibular angle where the body meets the ramus; sources differ on whether it is a midpoint or outermost inferior point.
Pogonion is the most anterior midline point of the chin; menton is the lowest median point of the chin; gnathion lies midway between pogonion and menton on the mandible (one source).
Sella is the centre of the pituitary fossa (sella turcica) of the sphenoid bone.
Downs and Steiner original definitions were not found in these searches; they need the original papers or a textbook.
Subnasale (sn) is where the columella meets the upper lip at the nasolabial contour; Nobel Biocare's 3D cephalometric guide defines it on the nasolabial contour between columella crest and upper lip.
Pronasale (prn) is the most anterior midpoint of the nasal tip (Nobel Biocare 3D soft-tissue definition); an Egyptian anthropometry study defines it as the most protrusive point in lateral view.

Subnasale is defined inconsistently: a CNN study calls it the deepest point at the nose base/upper lip junction, while the Egyptian study places it at the columella's lower border meeting the philtrum.

Labiale superius (ls) and labiale inferius (li) are the most prominent points of the upper and lower lips in a CNN 2D study, whereas the Egyptian study places ls at the midline of the upper vermilion border.
Stomion (sto) is where the upper and lips meet in the midline; a class III surgery AI study splits it into stomion superius (Stms) and inferius (Stmi).
Soft tissue gnathion (gn') is defined as the lowest midpoint of the chin soft-tissue contour in some sources, while others place gn at the neck-throat junction.

Exocanthion (ex) and endocanthion (en) are the outer and inner corners of each eye fissure in soft tissue; cheilion (ch) is the labial commissure; alare (al) is the most lateral point of the alar contour; trichion (tr) is the anterior hairline midline; vertex (v) is the highest midline point of the skull.

Farkas (1994, Anthropometry of the Head and Face) is cited as the standard reference for craniofacial landmark definitions and North American White male and female norms; many definitions are framed in 2D planes.
A 2019 study found considerable differences between Farkas norms and 3D stereophotogrammetry data, attributed possibly to measurement method, secular trends, or ethnic composition.
A 3D imaging study uses Farkas-style abbreviations: g, n, sn, pg, en, ex, al, cph, ch, ls, ft.
The MediaPipe Face Mesh model outputs 478 landmarks: the first 468 mesh points keep a stable order, with 10 iris points appended at indices 468-477.

A MIT-licensed community converter (PeizhiYan/Mediapipe_2_Dlib_Landmarks) maps MediaPipe 478 landmarks to dlib 68 landmarks via a single function; its index table was not visible in search results and must be checked in the repo.

dlib's 68-point detector outputs 68 (x,y) points trained on iBUG 300-W; tutorial index ranges (Python slices): jaw [0,17), right eyebrow [17,22), left eyebrow [22,27), nose [27,35), right eye [36,42), left eye [42,48), mouth [48,68).
The sources' range notation is end-exclusive slices; the inclusive per-point reading (jaw 0-16, mouth 48-67, etc.) is general knowledge of the dlib layout and was NOT confirmed by the search results.
dlib's 5-point model is a lower-density alternative and can be used as a drop-in in some sources' description.

Best-case 3D face-scan landmark error: a CNN approach reported overall mean 0.83 +/- 0.49 mm, with lowest error at endocanthion, exocanthion, cheilion; attribution URL not confirmed from the search output.
A non-rigid template registration on a 3D optical scanner gave landmark error <2 mm for 53.1% of landmarks and <4 mm for 84.4%; midface errors smallest, upper face largest.
A PCA method combining 3D geometry and 2D texture gave RMS about 1.7-1.8 mm over 17 landmarks.
Under large yaw and expression variation, a 3D landmark detection method reported 4.5-6.3 mm mean localization error.
A U-Net 3D facial landmark study reported average NME 2.8 mm in acromegaly patients, indicating accuracy needs improvement.
A mobile-device-compatible 3D scanner under controlled lighting and angles averaged about 1 mm error on facial landmarks.
Manual cephalometric identification shows high intra- and inter-operator variability, with errors possibly above 2 mm for gonion and orbitale.
In a 3D CBCT study gonion had the largest Euclidean intra- and inter-observer distances; gonion, nasion, orbitale and ANS had the greatest median distances.
In a CBCT observer study, gnathion, menton and pogonion ICCs were mostly 0.9 or above; gonion inter-observer Y-axis ICC was about 0.71-0.73.
Orbitale and porion are bilateral, so left and right images overlap, which can add error when locating midline-referenced points.
A 2025 CBCT commercial-software study found large gonion location errors but accurate FMA because the error ran along the gonion-menton line.
Gonion and orbitale mean errors of 1.06 mm and 1.39 mm respectively were reported in a deep-learning study; the source was not confirmed from search output.

Blender add-on FaceFit (VGCLUB/facefit-mpfb) is a v0.1 prototype that fits MPFB2 heads to photos using 57 stable points out of MediaPipe 478; solving runs in an external MCP server; tested on Blender 4.2.3 LTS with MPFB2 2.0.18.
CaptureForge (GPL-3.0) auto-rig needs a front view with visible eyes and mouth; its roadmap reports fitting tracked landmarks made weights worse than MediaPipe's own scores on stylized heads.
No 2025 benchmark for 3D or anthropometric face landmarks was found; the closest 2025 item, Proto-Former (Oct 2025), is a 2D method.
Infinite 3D Landmarks (2024) dropped jaw points on the Sagonas evaluation because its sliding jawline landmarks are not 3D consistent.

contradictions: Subnasale: Nobel Biocare (nasolabial contour between columella crest and lip) vs CNN study (deepest point at nose base/upper lip) vs Egyptian study (columella lower border meeting philtrum).
Labiale superius: CNN study (most prominent upper lip point) vs Egyptian study (midline of upper vermilion border).
Stomion: single point in 3D scanner study vs split into Stms/Stmi in class III AI study.
Gnathion (soft tissue gn'): lowest chin midpoint vs neck-throat junction in different sources.
Orbitale: lowest inferior orbital rim point vs midpoint between the two orbits' lowest inferior margins.
Gonion: midpoint vs outermost inferior point of the mandibular angle.
Farkas norms vs 3D stereophotogrammetry data differ considerably (2019 study).
